title: Billboards, Mailers, and Cold Feet: The Collapse of D.C.’s Bottle Bill
summary: For more than three years, Lora Nunn has spent her weekends hauling soggy plastic water bottles and crushed aluminum cans out of neighborhood blocks, rec center playgrounds, and clogged storm drains east of the Anacostia River. content: For more than three years, Lora Nunn has spent her weekends hauling soggy plastic water bottles and crushed aluminum cans out of neighborhood blocks, rec center playgrounds, and clogged storm drains east of the Anacostia River. During those cleanups, she has seen firsthand how east-of-the-river neighborhoods tend to bear the brunt of beverage litter. Knowing how big beverage corporations killed D.C.’s 1980s bottle bill campaign by arguing it would disproportionately burden Black and brown residents, Nunn recognized the playbook immediately when this year billboards and glossy mailers—featuring a Black woman staring worriedly at a long grocery receipt under the headline “GROCERY BILLS ARE ALREADY HIGH”—began saturating corridors and mailboxes specifically in Wards 5, 7, and 8, according to Nunn. Paid for by the American Beverage Association under the banner of the Alliance for an Affordable DC , the ads warned that D.C.’s proposed bottle deposit bill would hike the cost of a 24-pack of water by $2.40, force seniors to haul discarded cans to redemption sites, threaten small businesses, and bring a new trash transfer facility that increases truck traffic alongside “sanitation and pest” issues in local communities. Along the bottom of the mailer, voters were urged to call three specific lawmakers: Ward 7 Councilmember Wendell Felder and At-Large Councilmembers Elissa Silverman and Christina Henderson . “All of the concerns that are raised are generated by the American Beverage Association,” says Susan Schorr , co-chair of the Sierra Club D.C. Chapter’s Zero Waste Committee and a co-lead of the Return, Refund, and Recycle Coalition for DC (3RC for DC)—an alliance of more than 20 local environmental and community groups pushing for the deposit law. The American Beverage Association, the national trade lobby representing soda and bottled-water giants like Coca-Cola and PepsiCo, has spent millions fighting similar container deposit laws nationwide. “They take whatever the hot button issue of the day is and try to get people riled up about that.” It seems a multipronged pressure campaign effectively ran out the clock. Last week, on Nov. 20, Ward 1 Councilmember Brianne Nadeau confirmed that her Recycling Refund and Litter Reduction Amendment Act of 2025 will not advance before the two-year Council period ends in December—meaning the legislation dies without a vote and must be reintroduced from scratch in 2027. On Nov. 23, Carrie Kohns , a spokesperson for the Alliance for an Affordable D.C., reached out to City Paper in response to multiple interview requests to ABA and ABA representatives in the past month. In a statement emailed to City Paper on Nov. 24, Kohns wrote: “The Alliance for an Affordable DC ran a citywide campaign to make the public aware of an unprecedented bottle bill proposal that would have increased the cost of everyday beverages for residents and put more pressure on small businesses already struggling to stay afloat. “The risk of harm included tremendous costs to operate such a system and the necessity to site trash transfer facilities in vulnerable neighborhoods that would increase truck traffic and environmental burdens. All of these concerns were well known to those involved in the discussions of the proposal and we worked to make sure they were also understood across the District by the local business community, labor unions, community organizations and DC residents.” The lobbying group backed by ABA and ABA itself specifically did not respond to multiple emailed requests for comment on allegations of targeted advertising, the amount of money spent to fight the bill, and what alternative measures ABA supports to reduce beverage container litter in D.C., as well as ABA’s claims that the bill would bring a new “trash transfer station” to Wards 5, 7, and 8. (The same questions were sent to Kohns.) A mailer against the bottle bill. Photo credit: Lora Nunn The death of the legislation was an abrupt collapse for a bill that looked unstoppable on paper. When Nadeau introduced B26-0058 in January 2025 , 10 of the Council’s 13 members signed on as co-introducers—a veto-proof majority to place a 10-cent refundable deposit on glass, plastic, and aluminum beverage containers, with the intention of tackling beverage litter and boosting D.C.’s lagging recycling rate. Over the next 22 months, however, a multimillion-dollar lobbying blitz by national beverage giants—combined with warnings from D.C.’s few remaining local breweries that the bottle bill could squeeze their already thin margins—eroded that momentum until time ran out (unpassed bills automatically expire when the two-year Council session ends in December.) Under the filed proposal , beverage distributors would have funded a stewardship nonprofit to administer the program under the DC Department of Energy and Environment oversight, paying retailers a 4 cent handling fee per returned container while unclaimed deposits funded water filters for low-income residents, reverse vending machines , and public refill stations. Advocates pointed to brand audits conducted during Ward 7 and 8 cleanups showing that more than 55 percent of beverage containers sold in the District are plastic bottles, according to dat a cited by 3RC for DC—led by Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Deer Park, Anheuser-Busch, and Costco’s Kirkland brand—and that plastic bottles account for roughly 60 percent of the trash pulled from the Anacostia River . Nathan Harrington , executive director of Ward 8 Woods Conservancy, says his staff and volunteers have removed more than 1.6 million pounds of trash east of the river since 2018—more than half of it bottles and cans. “We don’t want to keep doing the same thing forever,” says Harrington. “We want to change the economics of how trash is managed so that we don’t have so much of it ending up on the ground and in our woods and in our streams.” But the beverage industry was not on board. It mounted a massive spending push —echoing its 2019 campaign against D.C.’s proposed soda tax —to stop the District from becoming the first jurisdiction in more than two decades to adopt a new container deposit law, and a potential domino for neighboring Maryland, where lawmakers have considered similar bills. According to Oct. 15 disclosures filed with D.C.’s Board of Ethics and Government Accountability, the American Beverage Association spent around $2 million in 2026 opposing the legislation , including close to $1.9 million on ads and publications alone. “They have spent, I think it’s up to $3 million now, trying to defeat this bill,” Nadeau tells City Paper . Beyond billboards, social media ads, and text blasts—alongside opposition sites like stopthedcbottlebill.com and dcdirtybottlebill.com —the campaign also strained grassroots relationships on the ground. Nunn says neighborhood convenience stores that previously partnered with advocates on local cleanups pulled back once the coalition began pushing the bottle bill. Advocates say the opposition’s central talking points don’t hold up. Ten states already run bottle deposit programs—proving that major beverage companies can operate under deposit rules without driving up grocery prices while pushing container recycling rates to an average of 84 percent , more than triple D.C.’s 24 percent rate. Schorr points to a Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection study —as well as her own price checks of 24-packs of Coca-Cola at Wegmans stores across D.C., Pennsylvania, Connecticut, and New York—showing beverage prices in deposit states are comparable to, and sometimes cheaper than, non-deposit states. Both Schorr and Harrington also dismiss warnings about noisy processing facilities opening in Wards 5, 7, or 8, noting that D.C. lacks cheap industrial land (they also pointed out that PepsiCo recently closed its bottling plant in nearby Hyattsville). Still, Nunn says the relentless lobbying—combined with opposition from Mayor Muriel Bowser —made several of council’s original co-introducers hesitant to risk a veto override. “We actually haven’t lost any [councilmembers] officially yet,” Nunn said shortly before the bill stalled on Nov. 20. “But there are some councilmembers who are leery now that they’ve gotten more and more pressure from the ABA directly or indirectly, and some who said that they might vote for it, but maybe not if the mayor vetoes it.” While advocates pinned the resistance on national beverage giants, the fight also exposed sharp friction between environmentalists and some of D.C.’s smallest local manufacturers—like Thor Cheston , co-founder of Right Proper Brewing Company. Right Proper is one of just three remaining packaging and distribution breweries in the District, alongside Atlas Brew Works and DC Brau, after a prolonged local hospitality downturn wiped out peers like Hellbender, City-State, and 3 Stars. Right Proper produces about 5,000 barrels of packaged beer a year—roughly 900,000 cans, about 60 percent of which are sold in D.C., according to Cheston. By his math, all three local breweries combined make up just one-half of 1 percent of all single-serve beverage containers sold in the city. “We are not the problem,” Cheston tells City Paper . Under the original January 2025 version of the bill, beverage makers had to pay a per-container fee to fund the program: a 3 cent-per-can charge on top of the 10-cent deposit that Cheston says would have wiped out Right Proper’s payroll within a year. A subsequent revision eliminated that direct charge but would have placed liabilities on the brewery’s balance sheet that its bank refused to allow, according to Cheston. Even worse, Cheston says, he first learned about the bottle bill from signature-gatherers at a farmers market rather than from lawmakers. “The fact that they either did not recognize that it would put small businesses out of business instantly, or they didn’t care, and they just considered us collateral damage—both of those are very scary,” says Cheston. Cheston credits Ward 6 Councilmember Charles Allen , who chairs the Committee on Transportation and the Environment, and Ward 5 Councilmember Zachary Parker with stepping in after a tense July roundtable to rewrite the draft to exempt small local producers. Yet Cheston says an exemption for breweries still wouldn’t protect Right Proper from getting squeezed through its wholesale partner, Premium Distributors, which is not exempt from the program—a supply-chain ripple beverage wholesalers have warned would hit distributors across the region. Risa Hirao , an attorney at Pascal, Weiss & Hirao who serves as president of the D.C. Association of Beverage Alcohol Wholesalers, warned in Food Trade News that the bill would create severe logistical hurdles for regional distributors, did not respond to two emailed requests for comment. If distributors or retailers raise prices across the board to cover deposit logistics, Cheston says, Right Proper cannot afford to cut its wholesale prices to absorb the difference. “Target them,” Cheston says of national giants like Coca-Cola, Pepsi, and Deer Park. “Then just leave our distributor out of it. Leave us out of it.” Cheston argues D.C. should invest in public education around its existing single-stream recycling program before imposing a system that threatens small manufacturers already operating on razor-thin margins. Right Proper, he notes, has covered its Ward 5 roof in solar panels—currently offsetting about half its annual energy use—and is spending $300,000 on upgrades including a system to cut its water usage by 50 percent. Cheston says these investments align with the brewery’s environmental business ethos and make long-term economic sense. Nadeau, however, pushes back against Cheston’s claim that small brewers were blindsided when the bill was drafted. “Some of that is factually inaccurate,” says Nadeau. “In fact, I worked with many different stakeholders before introduction of the bill, including some of the brewers that have been most vocal about this, and did a lot of work to lessen the burden on them. Councilmember Allen has done even more work to lessen the burden on them, and at the end of the day, the largest costs of this bill are going to be borne by the beverage industry, the bottling industry—the folks who have been polluting our community for decades.” Nadeau, who will be succeeded in Ward 1 come January by Councilmember-elect Aparna Raj , attributes the bill’s failure to advance this fall to end-of-session congestion and lawmakers wanting more time to absorb implementation details rather than a loss of support. Even so, she didn’t mince words about the role of national industry money in slowing the bill down. “When you have outside special interests like the American Beverage Association pouring millions of dollars into a city to spread misinformation to residents and scare them about a measure that would actually improve their lives, you really have to call that out,” Nadeau says. “We won’t be defeated,” she continues. “We’re just making sure we take our time so that everybody understands what we’re implementing.” Broader business groups also cheered the bill’s collapse. In a statement, DC Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Chinyere Hubbard called the decision a “positive development for the District’s business community, particularly our small businesses and local retailers already navigating rising costs and economic uncertainty.” “We support efforts to improve recycling and environmental sustainability, but those goals should not come at the expense of our local business economy,” Hubbard wrote. Advocates, however, say the fight is only paused until the next Council session begins in January. “While 3RC for DC is disappointed that the bottle bill will not move forward this legislative session, we have every confidence that, when it is reintroduced and passed next year, it will be the strongest bottle bill in the country, and that out-of-town billionaire corporations will finally clean up the pollution their products cause in our beautiful District,” Schorr wrote in a statement after the bill was tabled last week. For Cheston, the pause offers relief for his business’ future and a chance to rethink the city’s approach before a new bill could be introduced in 2027. “I would love to support a sustainable and responsible environmental initiative in the future,” says Cheston.

title: Striking Distance Bring D.C.’s Hardcore Scene to the Forefront
summary: The local band reunited with the goal of highlighting current acts, raising money for Palestine, and going out on a high note.
content: The first hardcore show Ambrose Nzams ever attended happened only three days after D.C.’s Striking Distance broke up. He didn’t expect to be booking one of their final reunion shows more than two decades later. “Sometimes I don’t know whether reunions are good or bad,” Nzams told City Paper , six days before the iconic hardcore band reconstituted on Friday, Nov. 20, to thrash the stage of Transmission alongside New York hardcore legends Straight Ahead . From the back room of Joint Custody, the punk-centric record shop where Nzams mans the counter most days, he says that he felt different this time. “I’m so interested in the now, but they’re still [part of] the present in a weird way.” Though their initial four-year run lasted only from 1999 to 2003, Striking Distance’s legacy has hung like a phantom over the District’s hardcore scene since. They’ve reunited before, most recently in 2022, but haven’t played D.C. since their original disbandment. “The last time we played, four years ago, we felt like there was something missing,” says Dave Byrd , 55, frontperson of Striking Distance and later of Set to Explode . “We played Baltimore and Richmond, but we didn’t play D.C.” The offer to hop on a bill with Straight Ahead was welcome, Byrd says, but he wanted a chance to platform the D.C. scene for its own merits. The Transmission bill only included one other D.C. band—openers Inversion —so with the help of a few District hardcore mainstays, he put together a second show for the following day. The Saturday gig—a benefit for Heal Palestine, a nonprofit that delivers relief to displaced families in Gaza—took place at St. Stephen and the Incarnation Episcopal Church. Striking Distance headlined with support from Corvo , Laughing Corpse , Seclusion , Psyop , Social Interest , Sluggo , and Draw a Blank . Striking Distance. Photo credit: Ash Newton “What I envisioned, even a few years ago, [was that] we’re going to go out with a very memorable show that showcases a lot of the current bands right now and benefits a noble cause,” says Byrd. At Saturday’s concert, the band’s generational impact was evidenced by the rabid dogpile of young showgoers that gathered around Byrd’s mic, including members of support acts Sluggo and Social Interest. Each band on the lineup contributed a unique aspect to the District underground, says Byrd. In addition to Striking Distance, the show was also a farewell for Corvo, the aggressive Spanish-language punkers who have been active since 2018. After their set, the band gave away an entire box of tapes for free, containing their first and only full-length LP, La Gran Plaga , which was released April 14. Other acts celebrated their debuts; openers Draw a Blank played their first show while Social Interest appeared for a secret set after their initiation at Pie Shop on Nov. 15. Byrd highlighted Psyop as “the prototypical D.C. punk … a little bit of Black Flag in there, a little bit of VOID , and very political, very outspoken, very weird. And that’s kind of my thing.” The political necessity of the show extended beyond its beneficiaries, says Byrd. “In the D.C. area, we’re more about the message than just the music,” he says. And that message is simple: “Be a part of your community and go do something.” “Some people have a sense that we’re coming here to raise the scene again,” he says. “Not at all—if anything, we want to draw attention to what’s currently going on. Baltimore’s been getting a lot of attention, Richmond’s been getting a lot of attention … I feel like D.C. has been in the background.”

title: The Needle: Lonnie Bunch Responds to Smithsonian Overhaul Plan, U.S. Marshals Have Arrested 20K in D.C., East Potomac Golf Course Block Extended Through Mid-Dec., and More
summary: The Needle gains two points today.
content: Don’t work on the subway baby : Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch spoke about the images ProPublica published of a Metro commuter working on a document titled “The Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan ,” which showed plans to create new guidelines for the institution’s content, overhaul its systems for grants and lending, and fire more than a dozen employees, mostly from the National Museum of American History. Bunch, who will leave the Smithsonian next month, told employees, “The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research, and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.” Plus one point for protecting the institution. +1 [ Post ] Unsafe and ugly : The U.S. Marshals Service announced it will reach 20,000 D.C. arrests since convicted felon and President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March 2025 to create the “D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force.” Since then, federal law enforcement from 29 agencies, including 3,000-plus National Guard members, have been deployed here. D.C. police data shows property crime is down but violent crime is up 11 percent compared with last year.. Minus one point for wasting our tax dollars and making us feel less safe . -1 [ NBC4 ] Staying the course : U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes extended her order that blocks the Trump administration from closing East Potomac golf course through Dec. 12. The course will remain open through mid-December and the administration is barred from closing the course. Reyes has ordered Jessica Bowron , the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify at a hearing on Dec. 8 about the D.C. Preservation League’s motion for an injunction that would block the closure of the course indefinitely as litigation continues. Plus one point for delays. +1 [ NBC News ] Departure : Maryland man Kilmar Ábrego García arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the U.S., ending his battle against the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. He was originally arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and sent to a prison in El Salvador; in recent months he fought the administration’s plan to deport him to Africa. His attorney called the move “a temporary departure” and says Abrego Garcia may still return to the U.S. where his wife and child are U.S. citizens but they don’t expect it to happen under Trump. Ábrego García’s immigration status in Spain isn’t clear. Minus one point for breaking up families and Trump’s obsession with this man. -1 [ AP ] Pass the popcorn : House Democrats are demanding Donald Trump Jr .’s venture capital firm 1789 Capital and four companies related to it (Polymarket, Juul, GrabAGun, and Hadrian Automation) turn over their records as Congress begins investigating their business dealings. Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin sent the requests for communications exchanged between the companies, 1789 Capital, and its executive team. The investigation will examine whether the businesses benefited from Trump administration contracts, regulatory decisions, or proposed rule adjustments. Plus two points, one for investigations and one for oversight. +2 [ Independent ] Tuesday’s Needle rating : -67 Today’s score: +2 Today’s Needle rating: -65

According to Rob Sheffield “200 Best Songs of the 1990s,” more than a few D.C. (and D.C.-adjacent acts) were among the greatest: Helium ’s 1995 song “Pat’s Trick” landed at No. 119, Mya ’s 1998 track “It’s All About Me” landed at No. 166, and songs by Nirvana and the Foo Fighters (featuring Springfield’s Dave Grohl ) appear as well, including the fairly obvious No. 1 song.
